story.title: Maine Democrats Set to Nominate Troy Jackson for Senate Race
story.summary: Maine Democrats are convening to select a Senate nominee to replace Graham Platner, with former state Senate President Troy Jackson expected to secure the nomination. Jackson, who comes from a logging family, is preparing to challenge Republican Senator Susan Collins in the upcoming election, which is being closely watched nationally. Collins has significantly outpaced Jackson in fundraising, raising over $16 million compared to Jackson's $1 million since entering the race.

explore_lenses.label: How will Democrats replace Platner?
explore_lenses.title: A party convention selects the replacement
explore_lenses.summary: Maine law allows a party to replace a primary nominee who withdrew by the statutory deadline; the Democratic convention is the party’s selection mechanism, but state filing still matters for the November ballot.

claims.text: Maine law permits a political committee to make a replacement nomination when a primary nominee withdraws by 5 p.m. on the second Monday in July; the replacement deadline is 5 p.m. on the fourth Monday in July.

The Maine Secretary of State lists July 27, 2026, at 5 p.m. as the filing deadline for replacement candidates, and says replacements will be added to the general-election candidate list as nominations are received.
More than 600 delegates elected through county party meetings are due to vote in Bangor; AP reported that Jackson’s campaign said more than 480 of 601 voting delegates had committed to him.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: A convention vote does not by itself establish that the state has received and accepted the replacement nomination; that status depends on the filing by July 27.

explore_lenses.label: What would Jackson bring to the race?
explore_lenses.title: A rural political veteran with progressive ties
explore_lenses.summary: Jackson combines a long Maine legislative record and logging-family background with close ties to Bernie Sanders-aligned politics. That profile is likely to be central both to his appeal and to Republican criticism.

claims.text: Jackson is a fifth-generation logger from northern Maine and served as Maine Senate president from 2018 through 2024; he previously served in the state House and Senate.
Jackson worked on Sanders’ 2016 presidential campaign and has backed policies including Medicare for All and abolishing ICE, according to AP.

Colby College government professor Dan Shea told ABC News that Jackson’s rural-Maine background could help because, in Shea’s view, Mainers are skeptical of candidates perceived as being from outside the state.

Collins characterized Jackson as aligned with socialism and called him a “Bernie Bro”; Jackson said his campaign is building a statewide movement for “working people.” These are competing campaign characterizations, not independently resolved descriptions.

explore_lenses.label: Can Jackson overcome Collins’ money lead?
explore_lenses.title: A large cash and time disadvantage
explore_lenses.summary: Collins entered the late-stage matchup with substantial reported receipts and cash on hand. Jackson’s campaign says it raised more than $1 million after he entered, but that figure has not yet been matched here to a comparable FEC reporting period.

claims.text: Collins’ principal campaign committee reported $16.17 million in total receipts and $11.04 million in cash on hand for January 1, 2025, through June 30, 2026.
Jackson’s campaign said it had raised more than $1 million since he entered the Senate race; that is a campaign-provided figure rather than an FEC total cited in the reporting.

Forecast: Dan Shea told ABC News that the contest would be a “very tight and tense race” over the remaining three months, while AP reported that the replacement nominee had fewer than four months to introduce themselves to voters.

related_stories.title: Trump Issues Order for Warnings on 'Inaccurate' History at Smithsonian
related_stories.summary: President Donald Trump has issued an executive order requiring the installation of signage at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. The signs will warn visitors about what the administration deems 'inaccurate historical information' within the museum. This move follows ongoing accusations from the Trump administration of anti-American bias in the museum's exhibits.

related_stories.title: Indian Education Minister Resigns Amid Youth Protests Over Exam Scandal
related_stories.summary: Dharmendra Pradhan has resigned as India's education minister following widespread protests by youth over exam paper leaks. The protests, led by a movement referred to as 'Cockroach,' culminated in celebrations among demonstrators after Pradhan's resignation was announced. The movement's leaders indicated that the government had accepted their demands, leading to the decision to end the protests.

related_stories.title: Democrats Select South Carolina for First Presidential Primary in 2028
related_stories.summary: The Democratic National Committee has recommended that South Carolina hold the first presidential primary for the 2028 election cycle. This decision marks a significant shift in the primary calendar, as South Carolina will replace Iowa as the opening contest. The move aims to prioritize representation among Black and Latino voters, with Nevada also scheduled for an early primary.

related_stories.title: International Criminal Court Votes to Remove Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan
related_stories.summary: The International Criminal Court (ICC) has voted to remove Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan amid allegations of sexual misconduct. The decision comes nearly two years after the allegations first emerged. Khan has denied the accusations, which include claims of engaging in an improper relationship with a junior staff member and attempting to prevent her from pursuing her complaint.
